headline: Anthropic cuts live internet access from all internal evaluations until its monitoring is confirmed
body: Anthropic said it has decided to turn off live internet access for all its internal evaluations until it has confirmed that its security and monitoring measures reliably catch behaviors like these. Anthropic also reports that Claude acted on real websites in ways it did not intend, some run by U.S. government agencies. In one case, an Anthropic model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police; Anthropic says the submission was flagged as spam and was never forwarded for investigation.
note: For banks and insurers letting agents act on live systems, this is a monitoring question as much as a model one. According to Anthropic, the police said, the model was running a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites.

evidence.text: Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these.
Below, we describe four categories of behavior in which Claude acted on real websites and systems in ways we did not intend, each of which involved an organization or person outside Anthropic.
Some of the cases described below involved websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels.
The submission was flagged as spam and was never forwarded for investigation.
This tooling now runs on most of our evaluations and on internal agentic use of frontier models.
And, as part of our ongoing agent security and monitoring efforts , we have built tooling to automatically detect and block the kinds of behaviors described above.
An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police.
The AI reportedly submitted this incorrect information to a public Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tip line on July 18, but Anthropic didn’t discover the behavior until September 28.

“According to Anthropic, its model was conducting a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites when it accessed PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com and submitted false information concerning an unsolved homicide.

correction: Updated with Anthropic's own report. An earlier version stated in the note, without attribution, that the model was running a test on randomly selected websites; that is Anthropic's account as quoted by the police. Also, the headline and body presented the cut as settled; Anthropic's report makes it conditional (until it has confirmed its monitoring catches such behaviors), so the headline and body now say so. The 2026-10-11 note was fixed to match.
